items.title: Kuchipudi & Andhra Performing / Folk Arts
items.body:
### Kuchipudi and Andhra's performing arts

**In one line**
Andhra's stage traditions run from the classical dance-drama Kuchipudi to a rich set of folk narrative forms like puppetry and ballad-singing.

**Why it is asked**
APPSC asks who codified Kuchipudi, its signature item, and the origin of folk forms such as Burrakatha and Tholu Bommalata.

**The story**
**Kuchipudi** began at Kuchipudi village on the Krishna, where the saint **Siddhendra Yogi** shaped a temple dance-drama performed only by men, who also played the female roles. Alongside this classical form, villages kept narrative folk arts alive — leather puppet shows, drum-and-tambura ballads and devotional storytelling — which later became tools of social and political messaging.

**Why it matters**
These forms are directly AP-weighted, and the all-male Kuchipudi tradition is a common statement-based trap.

**Picture it**

| Form | Nature |
|---|---|
| Tholu Bommalata | leather shadow-puppet play; Satavahana antiquity; GI 'AP Leather Puppetry' |
| Burrakatha | ballad narration to a tambura + 2 vanthalu; from Jangam Katha |
| Harikatha | devotional storytelling; pioneered in Telugu by Adibhatla Narayana Das |
| Oggu Katha | Saiva ballads by Yadava 'Oggu' priests |
| Yakshagana / Veedhi Natakam | folk dance-drama & street theatre |
| Perini Sivatandavam | vigorous male temple dance, revived by Nataraja Ramakrishna |

Kuchipudi's signature items are **Bhamakalapam** (on Satyabhama) and **Golla Kalapam**; Vedantam Satyanarayana Sarma was famed in female roles and Vedantam Lakshminarayana Sastry pioneered the solo form. Old dance treatises: Nrittaratnavali (Jayapa Senani, Kakatiya court) and Vasantarajiyam (Kumaragiri Reddi).

**Terms explained**
- **Dance-drama** — a performance that tells a story through dance and acting together.
- **Vanthalu** — the two companions who assist a Burrakatha narrator.
- **Jangam Katha** — the Vira Saiva balladry from which Burrakatha evolved.
- **GI tag** — Geographical Indication, a legal mark of regional origin.

**Don't confuse**
- **Kuchipudi (classical) vs Perini (folk)** — Kuchipudi is the recognised classical dance-drama; Perini Sivatandavam is a revived vigorous male temple dance.
- **Burrakatha vs Harikatha** — Burrakatha is a tambura ballad (from Jangam Katha); Harikatha is devotional storytelling pioneered by Adibhatla Narayana Das.

**Remember it**
'THolu-BURRa-HARI': THolu (leather puppets), BURRakatha (tambura ballad), HARIkatha (devotional narration).

**TL;DR**
- Kuchipudi: Siddhendra Yogi, Kuchipudi village, all-male tradition, Bhamakalapam.
- Tholu Bommalata = GI-tagged leather shadow puppetry of Satavahana antiquity.
- Burrakatha = tambura ballad from Jangam Katha; Harikatha = Adibhatla Narayana Das.
- Perini Sivatandavam = revived vigorous male temple dance.
keyPoints: Kuchipudi was systematised by Siddhendra Yogi (14th c.) at Kuchipudi village, Krishna district.
Bhamakalapam (on Satyabhama) is the signature Kuchipudi item; it was traditionally an all-male form.
Tholu Bommalata = leather shadow-puppet theatre of Satavahana antiquity, GI-tagged as AP Leather Puppetry.
Burrakatha = tambura ballad narration (lead + two vanthalu), evolved from the Vira Saiva Jangam Katha.
Harikatha was pioneered in Telugu by Adibhatla Narayana Das of the Vizianagaram court.

items.title: Handicrafts, Toys & Kalamkari
items.body:
### Andhra handicrafts, toys and Kalamkari

**In one line**
Andhra Pradesh is known for distinctive wooden toys, painted Kalamkari textiles and metal/instrument crafts, each tied to a particular town.

**Why it is asked**
Match-the-following items pair a craft centre with its product, and the two Kalamkari styles are a frequent swap-trap.

**The story**
Particular villages became famous for a single craft passed down through artisan families: one for soft-wood toys, another for lacquered toys, others for brass, veenas and painted cloth. **Kalamkari** cotton art survives in two distinct styles — one drawn entirely free-hand with a pen, the other printed with carved wooden blocks.

**Why it matters**
These crafts carry GI tags and are both heritage markers and rural livelihoods, making them examinable in Prelims and Mains alike.

**Picture it**

| Centre | District | Product / finish |
|---|---|---|
| Kondapalli | Krishna | soft Punki wood toys, water colours |
| Etikoppaka | Visakhapatnam | Ankudu wood, lac-turned (lacquer) toys |
| Tirupati | Tirupati (Chittoor) | hard red-sander wood, unpainted toys |
| Budithi | Srikakulam | bell-metal & brass ware |
| Bobbili | Vizianagaram | veena from a single jackwood log |
| Udayagiri | Nellore | wooden cutlery |

**Kalamkari:** the **Srikalahasti style** (Tirupati/Chittoor) is wholly **free-hand pen** work with Hindu temple themes; the **Machilipatnam style** (Pedana, Krishna) uses **block-printed** outlines and Persian motifs from the Golconda era. Both use natural/vegetable dyes with a mordant-and-resist process.

**Terms explained**
- **Lac-turned** — shaped on a lathe and coloured with lac (a natural resin).
- **Mordant** — a substance that fixes dye to cloth.
- **Resist process** — covering parts of cloth so they do not take the dye.
- **Kalam** — the pen used in free-hand Kalamkari.

**Don't confuse**
- **Srikalahasti vs Machilipatnam Kalamkari** — Srikalahasti is free-hand pen work; Machilipatnam is block-printed. APPSC often reverses these.
- **Kondapalli vs Etikoppaka** — Kondapalli = soft Punki-wood toys; Etikoppaka = lacquered Ankudu-wood toys.

**Remember it**
'Srikalahasti = Stylus (pen)' free-hand; 'Machilipatnam = Machine (block)' printed.

**TL;DR**
- Kondapalli toys = Punki wood (Krishna); Etikoppaka = lac-turned Ankudu wood (Visakhapatnam).
- Srikalahasti Kalamkari = free-hand pen; Machilipatnam = block-printed.
- Budithi = brass; Bobbili = veena; Udayagiri = wooden cutlery.
- Both Kalamkari styles use natural dyes with mordant-and-resist.
keyPoints: Kondapalli toys = soft Punki wood (Krishna dist.); Etikoppaka toys = lac-turned Ankudu wood (Visakhapatnam).
Srikalahasti Kalamkari is wholly free-hand temple art; Machilipatnam (Pedana) Kalamkari uses block-printed Persian-influenced outlines.
Budithi = bell-metal/brass (Srikakulam); Bobbili Veena from a single jackwood log (Vizianagaram); Udayagiri = wooden cutlery.
Both Kalamkari styles use natural/vegetable dyes with a mordant-and-resist process.
Kondapalli, Etikoppaka, Bobbili Veena, Budithi and both Kalamkari styles are GI-tagged.
items.source: History & Culture of the Andhras — Utility Arts; GI Registry

items.title: GI Tags & Handloom Textiles of Andhra Pradesh
items.body:
### GI tags and handloom textiles of AP

**In one line**
Andhra Pradesh holds many Geographical Indication (GI) tags across crafts, handloom sarees and farm produce, several of which split from Telangana after the 2014 bifurcation.

**Why it is asked**
APPSC asks which products are AP GI tags and pairs a handloom centre with its specialty saree.

**The story**
A **GI tag** legally ties a product to the place that makes it, protecting authenticity and the artisans' incomes. After the 2014 bifurcation some old combined-state GIs became Telangana's (Pochampally Ikat, Bidriware), while AP retained its own crafts, handloom clusters and farm goods. Each handloom town is known for a particular weave.

**Why it matters**
The GI list is a ready current-affairs and Mains-livelihood resource, and the saree-town pairings are classic match questions.

**Picture it**

| Centre | District | Specialty |
|---|---|---|
| Dharmavaram | Sri Sathya Sai (Anantapur) | silk sarees, broad gold-brocade borders |
| Venkatagiri | Tirupati (Nellore) | fine high-count cotton sarees |
| Uppada | Kakinada (E. Godavari) | Jamdani sarees |
| Mangalagiri | Guntur | cotton sarees with Nizam border |
| Chirala → Pochampally | Prakasam / (Telangana) | ikat / telia-rumal tie-and-dye |

**AP GI crafts/art:** Srikalahasti & Machilipatnam Kalamkari, Kondapalli Bommallu, Etikoppaka Toys, Bobbili Veena, Budithi Bell & Brass, AP Leather Puppetry (Tholu Bommalata), Udayagiri Wooden Cutlery. **AP GI food:** Banaganapalle Mangoes (2017), Tirupati Laddu (2009), Guntur Sannam Chilli, Araku Valley Arabica Coffee (with Odisha).

**Terms explained**
- **Geographical Indication (GI)** — a sign that a product comes from a specific place and has qualities due to that origin.
- **Jamdani** — a fine figured muslin weave.
- **Bifurcation** — the 2014 split of united Andhra Pradesh into AP and Telangana.
- **Telia-rumal** — an oil-treated tie-and-dye cloth linked to ikat.

**Don't confuse**
- **AP vs Telangana GIs** — Pochampally Ikat, Nirmal Toys, Gadwal Sarees and Bidriware are now Telangana's, not AP's.
- **Uppada vs Venkatagiri** — Uppada = Jamdani; Venkatagiri = fine cotton. Do not swap.

**Remember it**
Dharmavaram = silk + gold border; Uppada = Jamdani; Venkatagiri = fine cotton.

**TL;DR**
- GI tag = legal link of a product to its place of origin.
- AP food GIs: Banaganapalle mango (2017), Tirupati laddu (2009), Guntur chilli, Araku coffee.
- AP handloom: Dharmavaram silk, Venkatagiri cotton, Uppada Jamdani, Mangalagiri.
- Pochampally Ikat & Bidriware are now Telangana GIs after 2014.
keyPoints: AP GI crafts: Srikalahasti & Machilipatnam Kalamkari, Kondapalli Bommallu, Etikoppaka Toys, Bobbili Veena, Budithi Brass, AP Leather Puppetry.
AP GI food: Banaganapalle Mangoes (2017), Tirupati Laddu (2009), Guntur Sannam Chilli, Araku Valley Arabica Coffee.
AP GI handloom: Dharmavaram silk, Venkatagiri cotton, Uppada Jamdani, Mangalagiri sarees.
Pochampally Ikat, Nirmal Toys, Gadwal Sarees and Bidriware are now Telangana GIs after the 2014 bifurcation.
The ikat/telia-rumal tie-dye technique is traced to Chirala in the early 19th century.

items.title: Telugu Literature — Eras & Major Poets
items.body:
### Telugu literature — eras and poets

**In one line**
Telugu literature grew in clear stages, from the first inscriptions, through the Mahabharata trio and the Vijayanagara golden age, to the modern reformers.

**Why it is asked**
APPSC asks the first Telugu inscription, the Kavitrayam, the Golden Age court, and the modern prose pioneers.

**The story**
Telugu first appears in short records, then in a full inscription under the **Renati Cholas**, before three poets — Nannaya, Tikkana and Errana — rendered the Mahabharata into Telugu across three centuries. Under the Reddis and especially in **Krishnadeva Raya's** Vijayanagara court, Telugu reached its 'golden' Prabandha age. In the 19th–20th centuries, reformers moved it from classical to spoken style and into the modern novel and poetry.

**Why it matters**
This is core AP heritage, and the names/works are heavily tested in both Prelims and Mains.

**Picture it**

| Era | Poets & works |
|---|---|
| Kavitraya (11th–14th c.) | Nannaya (Adi Kavi) → Tikkana → Errana: Telugu Mahabharatam |
| Saiva/desi | Palkuriki Somanatha (dwipada), Nannichoda (jaanu tenugu) |
| Reddi era (15th c.) | Srinatha ('Kavi Sarvabhauma'), Potana (Bhagavatamu) |
| Prabandha Golden Age (16th c.) | Krishnadeva Raya & the Ashtadiggajas; Amuktamalyada; Allasani Peddana (Manu Charitramu); Tenali Ramakrishna |
| Bhakti/pada | Annamayya (pada kavita pitamaha), Kshetrayya, Bhadrachala Ramadas, Vemana (satakam) |
| Modern | Veeresalingam (prose renaissance), Gurajada (Kanyasulkam), Gidugu Ramamurti (vyavaharika movement), Sri Sri, Viswanatha Satyanarayana (Jnanpith 1970) |

First complete Telugu inscription: Renati Cholas, Erragudipadu (Kadapa), c. 575 CE; the script came from Brahmi via the Bhattiprolu variety (Guntur). Early women poets: Molla (Ramayanamu), Timmakka, Tarigonda Vengamamba.

**Terms explained**
- **Inscription** — writing carved on stone or metal.
- **Prabandha** — a Telugu long narrative poem, the hallmark of the Golden Age.
- **Vyavaharika** — the spoken form of Telugu (championed by Gidugu).
- **Jnanpith** — India's highest literary award.

**Don't confuse**
- **Kavitrayam vs Ashtadiggajas** — the Kavitrayam are the three Mahabharata poets; the Ashtadiggajas are the eight 16th-c. court poets.
- **Gidugu Ramamurti's side** — he championed the SPOKEN (vyavaharika) form, not the classical one.

**Remember it**
Mahabharata trio order 'NA-TI-E': Nannaya, Tikkana, Errana.

**TL;DR**
- First complete Telugu inscription = Renati Cholas (c. 575 CE, Kadapa).
- Kavitrayam = Nannaya + Tikkana + Errana (Telugu Mahabharatam).
- Golden Age: Krishnadeva Raya's Ashtadiggajas; Peddana wrote Manu Charitramu.
- Modern: Veeresalingam, Gurajada, Gidugu (spoken Telugu), Viswanatha (Jnanpith 1970).
keyPoints: First complete Telugu inscription = Renati Cholas, Erragudipadu (Kadapa), c. 575 CE.
Kavitrayam = Nannaya (Adi Kavi) + Tikkana + Errana, authors of the Telugu Mahabharatam.
16th-c. Golden/Prabandha Age: Krishnadeva Raya's Bhuvana Vijayam court of the Ashtadiggajas; he wrote Amuktamalyada.
Allasani Peddana ('Andhra Kavita Pitamaha') wrote Manu Charitramu; Annamayya is the father of pada kavita.
Modern era: Veeresalingam (prose renaissance), Gurajada (Kanyasulkam), Gidugu Ramamurti (spoken-Telugu movement), Sri Sri, Viswanatha Satyanarayana (Jnanpith 1970).
items.mnemonic: Mahabharata trio order 'NA-TI-E': NAnnaya, TIkkana, Errana.
items.source: History & Culture of the Andhras — Language & Literature

items.title: Buddhist Art & Temple Architecture of Andhra
items.body:
### Buddhist art and temple architecture of Andhra

**In one line**
Andhra has India's richest cluster of ancient Buddhist sites and a long line of temple-building dynasties from the Vishnukundis to Vijayanagara.

**Why it is asked**
APPSC asks the feature unique to Andhra stupas (ayaka pillars), the Amaravati school, and which dynasty built a given temple.

**The story**
Under the Satavahanas and Ikshvakus, Andhra became a great Buddhist land, its stupas marked by **ayaka pillars** found nowhere else, and its marble carving defining the **Amaravati school**. Later Hindu dynasties built temples in succession — Vishnukundi caves, Eastern Chalukya and Eastern Ganga shrines, Kakatiya and finally Vijayanagara masterpieces like Lepakshi.

**Why it matters**
Amaravati and Lepakshi are AP's signature heritage, and the ayaka-pillar fact is a reliable discriminator.

**Picture it**

| Dynasty | Temples |
|---|---|
| Vishnukundi | Undavalli & Mogalrajapuram cave temples (Vijayawada) |
| Eastern Chalukya | Biccavolu group; Bhimeswara at Draksharama & Bhimavaram |
| Eastern Ganga | Mukhalingam (Srikakulam), Kalinga/Orissan style |
| Kakatiya | Thousand Pillar temple (Hanumakonda) & Ramappa (now Telangana) |
| Vijayanagara | Lepakshi Virabhadra (hanging pillar, murals, monolithic Nandi), Tirupati, Tadipatri |
| Qutb Shahi | Indo-Islamic Charminar, Golconda (now Telangana) |

Buddhist sites: Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda (capital Vijayapuri, Ikshvaku centre), Bhattiprolu, Ghantasala, Salihundam, Thotlakonda, Bavikonda, Guntupalli. The Mahayana Avalokitesvara cult is believed to have originated in Andhra. The Gudimallam lingam (Chittoor) is among the earliest anthropomorphic Siva-lingas.

**Terms explained**
- **Stupa** — a dome-shaped Buddhist relic mound.
- **Ayaka pillars** — a set of five pillars on a platform at each cardinal side, unique to Andhra stupas.
- **Mahayana** — the 'Great Vehicle' branch of Buddhism.
- **Anthropomorphic lingam** — a Siva-linga carved with a human figure.

**Don't confuse**
- **Amaravati vs Sanchi** — Andhra's Amaravati stupa has ayaka pillars; Sanchi has toranas (gateways) and no ayaka pillars.
- **Lepakshi (Vijayanagara) vs Ramappa (Kakatiya)** — Lepakshi has the hanging pillar/murals; Ramappa is the Kakatiya UNESCO temple (now Telangana).

**Remember it**
Ayaka pillars = 'Andhra's signature' on a stupa; Lepakshi = hanging pillar + murals.

**TL;DR**
- Ayaka pillars (five per cardinal side) are unique to Andhra stupas (Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda).
- Amaravati = marble Buddhist school; Nagarjunakonda (Vijayapuri) = Ikshvaku centre.
- Temple dynasties: Vishnukundi, Eastern Chalukya, Eastern Ganga, Kakatiya, Vijayanagara.
- Lepakshi Virabhadra (Vijayanagara) = hanging pillar, murals, monolithic Nandi.
keyPoints: Ayaka pillars (five per cardinal side) are a feature unique to Andhra stupas — Amaravati & Nagarjunakonda.
The Amaravati school is a marble Buddhist sculptural tradition; Nagarjunakonda (Vijayapuri) was the Ikshvaku Buddhist centre.
Lepakshi Virabhadra temple (Vijayanagara) is famed for its hanging pillar, ceiling murals and monolithic Nandi.
Eastern Chalukyas built Draksharama/Bhimavaram Bhimeswara temples; Eastern Gangas built Mukhalingam in Kalinga style.
The Gudimallam lingam (Chittoor) is among the earliest anthropomorphic Siva-lingas in India.
items.source: History & Culture of the Andhras — Arts: Architecture & Sculpture

items.title: Major Temples, Pilgrimages & Festivals
items.body:
### Major temples, pilgrimages and festivals of AP

**In one line**
Andhra Pradesh has famous pilgrim temples to Vishnu, Siva and Sakti, and distinctive Telugu festivals like Ugadi and Sankranti.

**Why it is asked**
APPSC pairs a temple with its deity/feature and asks the meaning of Telugu festivals.

**The story**
Andhra's great temples honour different gods — Venkateswara (Vishnu) at Tirumala, Mallikarjuna (Siva) at Srisailam, Narasimha at Simhachalam — and some, like Srisailam, are special because they are both a Jyotirlinga and a Shakti Peetha. The Telugu year opens with Ugadi and peaks at the harvest festival Sankranti.

**Why it matters**
Temple-deity pairings and festival meanings are frequent one-mark items with AP weighting.

**Picture it**

| Temple | Place | Deity |
|---|---|---|
| Venkateswara (Balaji) | Tirumala–Tirupati | Vishnu |
| Mallikarjuna + Bhramaramba | Srisailam | Siva (jyotirlinga) + Sakti |
| Varaha-Narasimha | Simhachalam (Visakhapatnam) | Vishnu |
| Kalahastiswara (Vayu linga) | Srikalahasti | Siva |
| Kanaka Durga | Vijayawada | Sakti |
| Satyanarayana | Annavaram | Vishnu |
| Surya | Arasavalli (Srikakulam) | Sun |
| Kurma (tortoise) | Srikurmam | Vishnu |

**Festivals:** Ugadi — the Telugu New Year (first day of Chaitra); its ugadi pachadi blends six tastes to symbolise life's mixed nature. Makara Sankranti (c. 13–14 Jan) — the harvest 'pedda pandaga', the start of Uttarayana, with Sun worship. Bathukamma — a women's floral festival (chiefly Telangana).

**Terms explained**
- **Jyotirlinga** — one of twelve supreme Siva shrines.
- **Shakti Peetha** — a sacred seat of the Goddess.
- **Pancha Bhoota Sthalam** — a temple linked to one of the five elements (Srikalahasti = air/Vayu).
- **Uttarayana** — the northward journey of the Sun from mid-January.

**Don't confuse**
- **Srisailam's dual status** — it is unique as BOTH a Jyotirlinga and a Shakti Peetha.
- **Ugadi vs Sankranti** — Ugadi is the New Year (Chaitra, spring); Sankranti is the January harvest festival.

**Remember it**
Ugadi = year's start (Chaitra); Sankranti = harvest 'pedda pandaga' (January).

**TL;DR**
- Tirumala = Venkateswara (Vishnu); Srisailam = Mallikarjuna (Siva) + Bhramaramba (Sakti).
- Simhachalam = Varaha-Narasimha; Srikalahasti = Vayu linga (Siva).
- Ugadi = Telugu New Year (Chaitra); its pachadi mixes six tastes.
- Makara Sankranti (c. 13–14 Jan) = harvest festival, start of Uttarayana.
keyPoints: Tirumala = Venkateswara (Vishnu); Srisailam = Mallikarjuna (Siva jyotirlinga) with Bhramaramba Sakti.
Simhachalam = Varaha-Narasimha (Vishnu); Srikalahasti = Kalahastiswara (Siva, Vayu linga); Kanaka Durga = Vijayawada.
Annavaram = Satyanarayana; Arasavalli = Surya; Srikurmam = Kurma (tortoise) avatar of Vishnu.
Ugadi is the Telugu New Year (Chaitra); its ugadi pachadi mixes six tastes for life's blend of experiences.
Makara Sankranti (c. 13–14 Jan) is the harvest 'pedda pandaga' marking the start of Uttarayana.
items.mnemonic: Ugadi = year's start (Chaitra); Sankranti = harvest 'pedda pandaga' (January).
items.source: History & Culture of the Andhras — Society & Religion: Pilgrimages; Festivals

items.title: Recent Recognitions — GI Tags & Padma Awards (AP)
items.body:
### Recent recognitions — GI tags & Padma awards (AP)

**In one line**
Andhra Pradesh keeps adding Geographical Indication (GI) tags and national Padma awards, which make easy, up-to-date exam facts.

**Why it is asked**
Current-affairs items test the latest AP GI tag and recent Padma awardees from the state.

**The story**
Alongside its long-standing GI products, Andhra's **Ponduru handspun khadi** of Srikakulam won a fresh GI tag in December 2025, prized for its ultra-fine hand-spun cotton. In the same year the actor **Nandamuri Balakrishna** received a Padma Bhushan for Art.

**Why it matters**
These are the newest, most quotable AP culture facts, exactly the kind APPSC drops into a current-affairs question.

**Picture it**

| Product | Type |
|---|---|
| Ponduru handspun khadi (GI Dec 2025) | Handloom |
| Banaganapalle mango | Fruit |
| Araku coffee | Agriculture |
| Guntur Sannam chilli | Agriculture |
| Tirupati laddu | Foodstuff |
| Machilipatnam & Srikalahasti Kalamkari | Handicraft |
| Kondapalli & Etikoppaka toys | Handicraft |
| Uppada Jamdani, Venkatagiri, Mangalagiri | Handloom |

**Padma award (AP):** Padma Bhushan 2025 — Nandamuri Balakrishna (Art/Cinema).

**Terms explained**
- **GI tag** — a Geographical Indication, a legal mark that a product belongs to a particular place.
- **Khadi** — hand-spun, hand-woven cloth.
- **Padma Bhushan** — the third-highest civilian award of India.

**Don't confuse**
- **Ponduru khadi vs the older AP GIs** — Ponduru khadi is the newest (Dec 2025), separate from the long-standing mango/laddu/Kalamkari GIs.

**Remember it**
Newest AP GI = Ponduru khadi (Dec 2025); 2025 Padma Bhushan (Art) = Nandamuri Balakrishna.

**TL;DR**
- Ponduru handspun khadi (Srikakulam) got a GI tag in December 2025.
- Nandamuri Balakrishna received the Padma Bhushan 2025 for Art.
- Older AP GIs: Banaganapalle mango, Araku coffee, Guntur chilli, Tirupati laddu.
- Srikalahasti Kalamkari = free-hand pen; Machilipatnam = block-printed.
keyPoints: Ponduru handspun khadi (Srikakulam) received its GI tag in December 2025.
Nandamuri Balakrishna was awarded the Padma Bhushan in 2025 for Art.
AP GI products include Banaganapalle mango, Araku coffee, Guntur chilli and Tirupati laddu.
Srikalahasti Kalamkari is free-hand pen work; Machilipatnam Kalamkari is block-printed.

items.title: For Mains — Andhra Pradesh Art & Culture
items.body:
### For Mains — Andhra Pradesh Art & Culture

**In one line**
For Mains Paper-II (M2-6, M2-7, M2-8), present AP culture as a continuous story of royal patronage, synthesis and living heritage that still supports rural livelihoods.

**How Mains frames this topic**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Evolution | Buddhist Amaravati/Nagarjunakonda → temple dynasties → Vijayanagara golden age → modern renaissance |
| Features | ayaka pillars, Lepakshi murals, Kuchipudi, Kalamkari, GI crafts |
| Significance | patronage links literature + architecture; crafts as livelihood & soft power |
| Continuity | Telugu from Renati Cholas (c. 575 CE) to Viswanatha's Jnanpith (1970) |
| Challenges | artisan decline, machine imitation, weak market linkage, conservation gaps |
| Way forward | GI enforcement, cluster development, heritage tourism, intangible-heritage protection |

**Data points / examples to quote**
- First complete Telugu inscription: Renati Cholas, c. 575 CE (Kadapa).
- Krishnadeva Raya's Bhuvana Vijayam and the Ashtadiggajas; Peddana's Manu Charitramu.
- GI milestones: Tirupati laddu (2009), Banaganapalle mango (2017), Ponduru khadi (Dec 2025).
- Ramappa temple (Kakatiya) inscribed UNESCO 2021; Lepakshi hanging pillar and murals.

**Use in answers**
- Open by tying a cultural form to its royal patron, then argue 'patronage drove AP's golden ages'.
- Diagram idea: a timeline from Satavahana Buddhism → Vijayanagara → modern reformers.
